extracted.intended_audience: authors of Cochrane and other systematic reviews / meta-analysts of healthcare interventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing, presenting, and incorporating risk of bias and conflicts of interest for study results included in systematic reviews and meta-analyses of interventions (Cochrane reviews). Focuses on domain-based tools (RoB 2, ROBINS-I), handling non‑reporting biases, and how to use assessments in analyses and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess risk of bias for each study result contributing to a Summary of Findings outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the risk of bias for each study result contributing to an outcome in the 'Summary of findings' table. Risk of bias in individual study results should be explicitly considered to determine the extent to which findings can be believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess risk of bias in results for outcomes included in the Summary of findings table (typically seven or fewer patient‑important outcomes). It may not be feasible to assess every result available when many studies exist; focus on outcomes most important to patients. (MECIR C52: Assessing risk of bias — Mandatory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use RoB 2 for randomized trials (domain-based, result-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: For randomized trials the RoB 2 tool is the preferred tool: a domain-based tool that includes a fixed set of bias domains and signalling questions, and is typically applied to a specific result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RoB 2 focuses on risk of bias only, uses signalling questions to help judgement, and produces domain-level and overall judgements for each result. The structure is similar to ROBINS‑I for non‑randomized studies. Cochrane recommends RoB 2 for all randomized trials in new reviews, although use of the original RoB tool is acceptable temporarily while learning/implementation challenges remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on risk of bias (not a general 'quality' score or other concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use domain-based tools that assess risk of bias (systematic error) rather than composite quality scales mixing risk of bias with reporting quality, precision, applicability, ethics, or completeness of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid summary scores or quality scales: they mix different concepts and produce results that are hard to interpret and can materially alter meta-analysis conclusions. The tool should target the single concept of risk of bias and not include unrelated dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect information from multiple sources to inform risk-of-bias assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Information for assessing risk of bias can be found in published articles, trial registers, protocols, clinical study reports, and regulatory reviews; contacting investigators may also be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and use trial registries, protocols (e.g. ClinicalTrials.gov), clinical study reports and regulatory documents where available. When contacting investigators, use open-ended questions to reduce the risk of overly positive answers (example questions provided for randomization and blinding). State when judgements are based on information outside publicly available documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform risk‑of‑bias assessments independently in duplicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk‑of‑bias assessments should be performed independently by at least two people, with a pre-specified process for resolving disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate assessment reduces errors and individual bias. Define how disagreements will be resolved (discussion, third‑party adjudication). Assessors should have content or methodological expertise. (MECIR C53: Assessing risk of bias in duplicate — Mandatory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide transparent support for each judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify judgements of risk of bias (low, high, some concerns) and provide this information in risk‑of‑bias tables as 'Support for judgement'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasons and, where possible, direct quotes from study reports, and explain why a method is flawed. Transparency allows readers, editors and referees to see why a particular judgement was made. (MECIR C54: Supporting judgements — Mandatory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Record sources of information for each risk‑of‑bias judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and report the precise source of information (e.g. quotation, summary from trial report, correspondence) that informed each judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the exact location within documents that informed the judgement. If judgements are based on information outside publicly available documents, state this. (MECIR C55: Providing sources of information — Mandatory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Present risk‑of‑bias assessments clearly and make full details available
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk‑of‑bias assessments may be presented in various formats; full tables with signalling question responses and supporting text should be made available for reference (often as supplementary material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not usually include lengthy full tables in the main body of the review. Use forest plots presenting RoB judgements alongside study results to give a visual impression of contributions at different levels of bias; optionally stratify/order by domain judgements or overall judgement. Consider bar graphs illustrating relative contributions of studies at each judgement, and when dividing bars prefer to weight by statistical information (precision or meta‑analysis weight) rather than number of studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make summary and overall judgements of risk of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit summary judgements about the risk of bias for important results both within studies and across studies; use the overall judgements produced by RoB 2 or ROBINS‑I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall judgements for a result are derived from domain assessments (see RoB 2/ROBINS‑I guidance). To summarize risk of bias across study results in a synthesis, follow guidance for assessing certainty in the body of evidence (e.g. GRADE) and explicitly report the summary assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess risk of bias due to missing results (non‑reporting/publication biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess risk of bias in a synthesis resulting from the absence of results from studies that should have been included (non‑reporting biases such as publication bias, selective reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑reporting bias can cause syntheses to over‑ or under‑estimate intervention effects. Consider types of reporting bias (publication bias, time‑lag bias, language bias, citation bias, multiple/duplicate publication bias, location bias, selective reporting). Use trial registries, cohorts with full accounting, and other methods to detect and address missing results (further methods described elsewhere in the Handbook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record trial characteristics not captured by RoB tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically record characteristics such as trial registration status, sample size, and single‑centre vs multi‑centre status in the 'Characteristics of included studies' table even if they are not included in risk‑of‑bias tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some features (e.g. single‑centre, small sample size, retrospective registration) may be associated with different effect estimates, they are not directly captured by RoB tools. Record them to support exploration of heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical evidence to inform risk‑of‑bias judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of empirical findings that specific methodological shortcomings (e.g. inadequate randomization, allocation concealment, lack of blinding) are associated with biased effect estimates, and that the influence varies by outcome type (larger for subjective outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate knowledge from meta‑epidemiologic studies (e.g. lack of allocation concealment and lack of blinding tend to exaggerate effects; subjective outcomes are more susceptible). Use such evidence to inform judgements but continue to assess risk of bias (not certainty of bias) for individual results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider conflicts of interest and source of funding of included studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and extract information on study funding and authors' conflicts of interest, as these may inform exploration of directness, heterogeneity, risk of bias within studies, and risk of bias in syntheses owing to missing results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators or funders with financial interests may influence design, conduct, analysis, or reporting (e.g. excluding unfavourable participants, failing to report unfavourable results). Review authors should seek funding and COI statements from trial reports and other sources, report them (e.g. in Characteristics of included studies), and consider them in analysis and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical approach to identifying and extracting conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically identify and extract details about funding sources, authors' declared conflicts, sponsor involvement, employment, stock ownership, consultancies and other relevant interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, validate declarations against external sources (e.g. Open Payments) and record characteristics of conflicts. Use the extracted information to inform subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, or to flag notable concern about potential bias arising from conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge whether conflicts of interest raise notable concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an explicit judgement about whether identified conflicts of interest constitute a 'notable concern' that could have influenced trial design, conduct, analysis, or reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assessment is useful for exploring heterogeneity between trials (e.g. subgroup analysis) and for reflecting on mechanisms by which COI may have biased study or synthesis results. Report concerns in the Characteristics of included studies table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk‑of‑bias assessment should be result‑specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments are typically specific to a particular result (e.g. particular outcome or analysis) because risk of bias may differ for different outcomes or analytical approaches within the same study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, two analyses for a single outcome (adjusted vs unadjusted) may have different risks of bias. Apply domain judgements to the particular result being considered rather than to the study as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot the risk‑of‑bias tool and provide training to improve reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Piloting the tool on a sample of articles and providing standardized training can improve reliability of assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot on about three to six papers to ensure consistent application of criteria and to help reach consensus. Standardized training has evidence of improving reliability. Do not rely on reporting statistical agreement (kappa); instead explore and resolve reasons for disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automation/machine learning cautiously to assist assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel methods (machine learning systems) can semi‑automate risk‑of‑bias assessment and extract supporting text but have limitations in reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some tools can identify relevant sentences and may reduce human workload (one study suggested about one‑third of articles could be assessed by one reviewer when using such tools). However, reliability compared with human reviewers is slight to moderate depending on domain; use with caution and human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using kappa statistics to describe agreement of duplicate assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not recommend the use of statistical measures of agreement (such as kappa) to describe the extent to which multiple authors' assessments were the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is more important to explore reasons for disagreement and resolve them than to report a kappa statistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate risk‑of‑bias assessments into analyses and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use risk‑of‑bias assessments to inform analyses (e.g. explore heterogeneity, perform sensitivity analyses excluding high‑risk studies, subgroup analyses, meta‑regression, or bias‑adjustment models) and the interpretation of synthesized results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk of bias in included studies and risk of bias due to missing results should influence how meta‑analysis results are interpreted and reported. Consider and report any analyses that investigate the impact of study-level risk-of-bias characteristics on pooled estimates (further methodological options described in Chapter 7 Section 7.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and report transparent processes and documentation for risk‑of‑bias work
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the process for reaching risk‑of‑bias judgements transparent and document sources, justifications, resolution of disagreements, and where full assessments are stored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide access to full risk‑of‑bias tables (supporting text, signalling question answers), record the source and precise location of supporting information, and state when judgements are based on assumptions or non‑public information.
